titre: What Rosalind Franklin knew, and is still denied
accroche: The common account makes her a victim robbed of a photograph. Rediscovered documents describe something else
contenu_vulgarise:
The story has become so familiar that it is told without thinking. Rosalind Franklin obtains at King's College a diffraction image of DNA, known as Photograph 51. Her colleague Maurice Wilkins shows it to James Watson without her knowledge. Watson immediately sees the helix, rushes to Cambridge, and publishes with Crick the structure of DNA. Franklin, robbed, dies at thirty-seven without knowing what was taken from her.

Two historians of science reopened the case in 2023, with documents previously unexploited. Their conclusion does not rehabilitate Watson and Crick. It challenges the role assigned to Franklin.

## What the documents show

The first is a letter addressed to Crick by a female colleague of Franklin's. The second is a press article written in 1953, which remained unpublished.

They show that the two teams, King's College and the Cavendish, worked far more in cooperation than the rivalry narrative suggests. That Franklin knew what her image implied, and that she was moving toward the helical structure. And that the sharing of information was, at least in part, known and organized.

It was Watson, not Crick, to whom Wilkins showed Photograph 51, a detail the common story erases, though it changes who saw what, and when.

## What the victim narrative costs

The two authors' argument deserves to be followed, because it is not the one you would expect.

To make Franklin a victim, they say, is to take away what she did. A victim endures; she does not work. The theft narrative turns her into the producer of data that others would have known how to read, which is exactly the subordinate role assigned to women in the laboratories of the time.

The documents describe a researcher who ran her own program, understood her results, and contributed to the solution as a full participant.

## What remains true

None of this erases the sexism at King's College, real and documented, nor the tone in which Watson speaks of her in his memoir, a caricature that did much to establish the image of a stubborn technician.

The 1962 Nobel Prize could not have gone to her in any case: it is not awarded posthumously, and she had died in 1958.

What this case shifts is more general. A very real injustice produced a compensatory narrative, itself inaccurate, and the compensatory narrative diminishes the person it claims to rehabilitate.

Doing justice to someone begins with describing what they did.

repere.texte: A letter addressed to Crick and an unpublished 1953 press article show that Franklin knew what her image implied, and that the two teams were cooperating.
repere.source: Cobb & Comfort, “What Rosalind Franklin truly contributed to the discovery of DNA's structure,” Nature, 2023

carte.punch: The theft narrative turns her into a supplier of data that others would have known how to read.
carte.idee: Rosalind Franklin is said to have been robbed of her Photograph 51. Documents found in 2023 describe a researcher who knew what her image implied, in two teams that cooperated more than they competed.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Nature — How Rosalind Franklin's story was rewritten
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English; traces how the narrative of dispossession was built after the fact.

quiz.question: What do the two historians fault the common account for?
choix: Exaggerating the sexism Franklin faced at King's College
Making Franklin a passive victim rather than a researcher who ran her own program
Crediting Watson and Crick with a discovery that belonged entirely to Franklin
Wrongly claiming that the 1962 Nobel could have been awarded to her
quiz.explication: Their argument is not to rehabilitate Watson and Crick: the sexism in the laboratory is real and documented. It is that the theft narrative reduces Franklin to a producer of data that others would have known how to read, precisely the subordinate role then assigned to women. The documents show that she knew what her image implied.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the documents found in 2023, to whom did Maurice Wilkins show Photograph 51?
choix: To Francis Crick, who then passed it on to Watson
To neither, the photo having been published before they saw it
To both at the same time, at a joint meeting
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is to Watson, not to Crick, that Wilkins shows Photograph 51, a detail the common story erases.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What documents do the two historians Cobb and Comfort rely on for their 2023 reassessment?
choix: A Franklin laboratory notebook found in the King's College archives
A posthumous interview with Watson given in 2020
A letter addressed to Crick and an unpublished 1953 press article
The original minutes of the 1962 Nobel committee
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A letter to Crick from a female colleague of Franklin's and an unpublished 1953 press article are the two previously unexploited documents on which their reassessment rests.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why could Rosalind Franklin not receive the 1962 Nobel Prize?
choix: Because the Nobel committee judged her contribution insufficient compared with that of Watson and Crick
Because she had explicitly refused to be associated with the discovery
Because the rules of the time excluded women from the hard sciences
Because the Nobel Prize is not awarded posthumously, and she had died in 1958
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Nobel Prize is not awarded posthumously, and Franklin, who died in 1958, could not have received it in 1962 in any case.
